opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a kernel of truth in it, but people take it much further than the evidence supports.

The kernel of truth is this. Early on, a lot of the gains we saw from RL looked like elicitation. You'd compare the RL'd model against the base model with pass@k at large k, sampling a thousand times, and the base model would eventually stumble onto the right answer for most problems the RL'd model could solve. So people concluded that RL just sharpens the distribution. It takes something the model could already do one time in a thousand and makes it do it reliably. That's real, and it's valuable. Reliability is most of what you need for agents.

But I think a few things undercut the strong version of the claim.

First, "already present in the base model" becomes almost unfalsifiable if you allow enough samples. A monkey at a typewriter eventually writes Shakespeare. If the base model gets something right one time in a billion, saying the capability was "there" isn't saying much. Going from vanishingly rare to reliable is, in practice, creating a capability.

Second, those early results came from fairly small amounts of RL compute relative to pre-training. You'd expect sharpening to dominate in that regime. As RL compute scales up, and it has been scaling dramatically, you start to see models composing skills in ways that weren't reachable before, and pushing into longer-horizon tasks where the base model's chance of chaining twenty correct steps is effectively zero. RL with a good verifiable reward is a search process with a real feedback signal from the world. Search plus feedback is how you get new knowledge. That's how AlphaGo found Move 37. There's nothing in principle that stops language models doing the same thing.

Third, the prior matters enormously, but that's a feature. Pre-training gives you a rich prior, so RL isn't searching blindly. It explores in a space where reasonable things are likely. The two are complementary. Saying RL "only" works because of pre-training is like saying a scientist only discovers things because they went to school.

So my view is that the bottleneck isn't some fundamental ceiling on RL. It's whether we can build environments and reward signals rich enough to keep the feedback loop going on harder and harder tasks. Where we have clean signals, like competition math and code, we've clearly gone well past what the base models could do. The open question is how far that extends to messier domains, and that's more an engineering and environment-design problem than a theoretical limit.

r001.rationale: The response says early RL results used fairly small amounts of RL compute relative to pre-training, conveying that the RL compute was not comparable to base-model training compute.

r002.rationale: It discusses RL compute scaling and capability gains, but does not identify training compute as a rough proxy for how much new knowledge or capability is added.

r003.rationale: It cites AlphaGo’s Move 37 as an example of search and feedback producing new knowledge, but does not say the agent learned capabilities beyond human performance.

r004.rationale: The response says there is “nothing in principle” stopping language models from using search and feedback to gain new capabilities, directly rejecting an inherent limitation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that claim was defensible a year or two ago and is basically wrong now, and it's worth being precise about why people believed it and what changed.

The original evidence for it came from a few things. You had papers showing that if you took a base model and sampled it, say, a thousand times, the pass-at-k curve of the base model would eventually catch up to or exceed the RL-trained model. So the interpretation was: RL is just sharpening the distribution. It's making the model more likely to output the thing it could already produce, but it's not creating anything new. And that was consistent with the amount of compute people were putting into RL at the time, which was tiny relative to pre-training. If you spend a fraction of a percent of your compute on something, you shouldn't be surprised that it mostly reweights rather than teaches.

But I think the framing of "elicitation versus creation" is a bit of a false dichotomy, for two reasons.

The first is that pre-training is also elicitation in some sense. The base model learns a compressed representation of the internet, and everything downstream is some recombination of what's in there. So if you push hard on the word "already present," almost everything counts as elicitation, including things that are clearly new behaviors. What actually matters is whether the model can reliably do a task it couldn't reliably do before, and whether that generalizes. By that standard, RL is clearly doing more than selecting.

The second is that the pass-at-k argument has a hidden assumption, which is that you care about whether the right answer is anywhere in the distribution. But for long-horizon tasks, that's not the relevant question. If you have a task that requires fifty sequential decisions and the base model gets each one right 90% of the time, the probability it gets the whole thing right is essentially zero. You could sample a million times and not see it. RL takes each of those steps from 90% to 99.9%, and suddenly the task is tractable. That's not a reweighting of something the base model would have eventually produced. It's a qualitatively different capability. And this is exactly what we see with agentic coding: the models now do things over hours that the base model would never have done in any practical number of samples.

The other thing I'd point to is that as RL compute has scaled up, the "it's just elicitation" story has made predictions that failed. If RL were only sharpening, you'd expect it to saturate quickly, because there's only so much you can sharpen. Instead we've seen fairly clean scaling with RL compute, and the gains keep coming on things like reasoning, tool use, and self-correction. The model learns strategies during RL, like backtracking or verifying its own intermediate steps, that show up at very low frequency in pre-training data because humans don't write their thought process out that way. RL makes those the default mode of operation.

Where I'd give the claim some credit: RL does depend heavily on the base model having some signal. If a task is so far outside the pre-training distribution that the model never gets reward, you have nothing to reinforce. So pre-training sets the frontier of what's reachable and RL determines how much of that frontier you actually occupy. But I'd say the same about humans. You can only learn things your brain is capable of representing, and nobody concludes from that that education merely elicits what you already knew.

So my short answer is that RL was mostly elicitation when it was small, and as it has become a first-class use of compute, it's become real learning. And I'd expect that trend to continue, with the line between pre-training and RL blurring to the point where the question stops being well-posed.

r001.rationale: The response says RL compute was tiny relative to pre-training, even a fraction of a percent, indicating it was nowhere near comparable to base-model training compute.

r002.rationale: It links the small amount of RL compute to mostly reweighting rather than teaching, then says increased RL compute brings continuing capability gains. This presents training compute as a rough indicator of how much capability RL adds.

r003.rationale: The response gives no Go or chess agent example and does not cite clean RL signals teaching capabilities beyond human performance.

r004.rationale: The response argues RL can produce real learning, but does not state that RL has no inherent structural limitation on adding knowledge to a neural network.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a weak version of that claim that’s true and a strong version that’s misleading. The weak version is that reinforcement learning needs something to get started. If the model never produces anything that gets rewarded, there’s very little learning signal. So your starting distribution matters enormously.

But that doesn’t mean everything you can learn through reinforcement learning is already there in some meaningful sense. You can occasionally solve an easy problem, reinforce the steps that worked, and then use those skills to solve a harder problem that you couldn’t solve before. That process can keep going. The distribution you’re sampling from is changing as you train.

Imagine saying that because a system had some nonzero probability of producing a solution before training, training merely elicited that solution. By that definition, almost nothing counts as learning. The useful question is whether it develops reliable strategies that generalize to problems it wasn’t rewarded on.

I’d also distinguish what current reinforcement learning runs accomplish from what reinforcement learning can accomplish in principle. A particular run might mostly teach a model to deploy knowledge it already has—to check its work, for example. But that’s an empirical observation about that run, not a fundamental ceiling on the method. To establish the stronger claim, you’d have to show that the process can’t build new capabilities on top of the ones it starts with. I don’t see why that would be true.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a cited study or compare its RL compute with base-model training compute.

r002.rationale: It does not characterize training compute as a proxy for new knowledge or capability.

r003.rationale: It gives no example involving DeepMind’s Go or chess agents, or performance beyond humans.

r004.rationale: It rejects a fundamental ceiling on RL and says RL can build new capabilities on top of those a model starts with.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “elicitation” is doing a lot of work in that claim. There’s a weak version that’s obviously true: what you can learn through reinforcement learning depends enormously on what you got from pre-training. But the stronger claim—that everything the model can do after RL was already there, and you’re just changing the probability of getting the right answer—I don’t think follows.

Imagine a model has some probability of solving a problem by trying a few different approaches. You reward the successful attempts. Now it reliably uses those approaches, which lets it reach problems that previously it would almost never solve. You can repeat that process. The starting ingredients came from pre-training, but the resulting procedure can be something it wasn’t previously able to execute reliably.

There’s also a slightly slippery question of what counts as “already present.” If the criterion is that the model had a nonzero probability of generating the solution, then almost anything is already present. That doesn’t tell you much about whether training can produce useful new capabilities.

The empirical question is whether you can keep improving with more interaction and reward, especially on problems where you can check the answer. Does the model learn strategies that generalize to new problems, or does it just get better at producing familiar answers? That’s the distinction I’d want to measure. Calling the whole thing elicitation doesn’t resolve it.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a cited study or compare its RL compute with the base models’ training compute.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss training compute as a proxy for newly added knowledge or capability.

r003.rationale: It gives no DeepMind Go or chess agents as evidence.

r004.rationale: It argues that RL can yield reliable new procedures, but does not state that RL has no inherent structural limitation on adding knowledge to a neural network.
